title: Nurturing Post-Disaster Emotional Adaptability in Young Learners: Socio-Cultural, Kinship, and Pedagogical Pathways in West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia
content: Purpose: This paper explores how post‐disaster emotional resilience develops among young children in West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia, analyzing how intertwined family, community, and cultural ecosystems mitigate developmental trauma in settings with limited psychosocial infrastructure. Method: Adopting an interpretative qualitative phenomenological approach, data were gathered from 38 purposively sampled informants—early childhood education (ECE) teachers, parents, school principals, religious and community leaders, and young children—via 94 in‐depth semi‐structured interviews, 96 naturalistic classroom observations over an eight‐week field immersion, projective play activities, and institutional archive reviews. Results: Empirical findings show that young learnersʹ psychological adaptability operates not as a solitary dyadic response, but through an integrated Triadic Resilience Ecosystem. Dependable emotional bonds within extended Sasak kinship networks form the core protective layer, actively strengthened by spiritual transmission practices and trauma‐informed hybrid pedagogies inside predictable preschool classrooms that curb developmental regression. Implications: Restoring foundational emotional well‐being in disaster‐prone areas calls for reorienting educational emergency policies beyond structural evacuation drills toward culturally grounded, trauma‐responsive early childhood curricula.
